headline: Certificate revocation lists can now be linted against the RFC 5280 profile.
summary: The lint engine read certificates and nothing else, so a CRL arriving from another issuer could only be parsed or path-validated, never surveyed for the profile rules RFC 5280 section 5 states. pki.lint.crl reports those rules as graded advisory findings, in the same report shape pki.lint.certificate returns and with the same promise that the data path never throws.

Added: pki.lint.crl(pem | der | parsed, opts) lints a certificate revocation list against RFC 5280 section 5, under the new profile name rfc5280-crl. It returns the same LintReport as pki.lint.certificate, and hostile bytes produce a single fatal lint/unparseable finding carrying the strict parser's code rather than raising.

On the CRL itself: nextUpdate presence (section 5.1.2.5) and thisUpdate not following it; cRLNumber presence, and the 20-octet ceiling section 5.2.3 places on a CRL number, measured on both the cRLNumber and the baseCRLNumber a delta CRL carries, which section 5.2.4 defines as a CRLNumber; both halves of the authorityKeyIdentifier requirement, that it is present and that it uses the key identifier method (section 5.2.1); the criticality every profiled extension must carry (section 5.2), with issuerAltName reported separately at warn because section 5.2.2 states its criticality as a recommendation; freshestCRL in a delta CRL (section 5.2.6); a delta whose cRLNumber does not exceed its baseCRLNumber (section 5.2.4); an issuingDistributionPoint stating a scope the profile does not permit (section 5.2.5); and an unrecognized critical extension.

On each revoked entry: the entry-extension criticality section 5.3 requires; a certificate serial that is not positive or runs past 20 octets, the same section 4.1.2.2 profile a certificate's own serial carries; a removeFromCRL reason code outside a delta CRL (section 5.3.1); a certificateIssuer on a CRL that declares itself direct, or one that omits the issuer distinguished name the clause requires (section 5.3.3); a reasonCode encoding unspecified(0), which section 5.3.1 says should be absent instead, at warn, and as an error where the CRL is scoped to some reason codes, since section 5.2.5 makes a meaningful reason a requirement there; a reason the CRL's own issuingDistributionPoint does not declare, where that extension names at least one reason (section 5.2.5); a scope naming none, which a mask that is empty or sets only the unused bit states, is reported against the extension rather than against every entry in turn; a serial listed twice on a direct CRL, where a reader cannot tell which entry governs (section 5.1.2.6); and an unrecognized critical entry extension.

An extension the section 5 profile names, whose value does not read as the structure that identifier names, is reported in either scope. Only extensions the CRL profile names are read this way: a certificate-only extension carried on a CRL is an unrecognized one, which the profile lets a consumer ignore when it is non-critical and which the unknown-critical row reports when it is not. Recognizing an extension by its identifier says only that the profile names it, so without this a critical issuingDistributionPoint carrying a NULL satisfied the criticality rule, was not an unrecognized extension, and reported clean although no consumer can process it. The issuingDistributionPoint is read through the same decoder certification-path validation uses, so the two verbs cannot disagree about what a well-formed one is. Where that extension does not read, the CRL states neither a scope nor a direction, so the rows that depend on it stand aside and the extension is reported once rather than every entry that would have followed from it.

pki.lint.rules("rfc5280-crl") enumerates the CRL registry, and pki.lint.rules() with no argument now returns the certificate and CRL rules together. The two verbs do not accept each other's profile names: passing a CRL profile to pki.lint.certificate, or a certificate profile to pki.lint.crl, raises lint/unknown-profile naming the verb to use instead.
Changed: Four section 5 rules have no row, because the strict parser refuses them before a rule could run: a CRL whose version does not match the extensions it carries (section 5.1.2.1), an empty issuer name (section 5.1.2.3), a present-but-empty revokedCertificates (section 5.1.2.6), and an extension repeated on the CRL or on an entry (section 4.2). Each reaches a caller as the fatal lint/unparseable finding carrying the parser's own code.
